Looking at a network is often the quickest way to understand it: a drawing shows at a glance
whether a graph falls apart into groups, has a few dominant hubs, or is a long chain. EdgeCase draws
graphs with `plot()`, which computes a layout and renders the graph as a self-contained SVG image.
The image needs no JavaScript to display, so it works the same in a Jupyter notebook, a Quarto
document, a web page, or a file on disk.

This page covers the mechanics of `plot()`: what it returns, how to save a drawing, and how to
control its size, labels, edges, and theme. The pages that follow go further:
[Layouts](layouts.qmd) describes the algorithms that place the nodes,
[Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd) maps colors and sizes to data, and
[Interactive widgets](interactive.qmd) covers the zoomable, draggable alternatives.

## A first plot

With no arguments, `plot()` places the nodes with a force-directed layout and draws every node and
edge. The karate club makes a good first example. `label_by="label"` shows the node labels, the
member numbers `"0"` to `"33"`, instead of the internal node IDs, and `seed=` fixes the random
starting positions of the layout so that the picture is the same every time:

::: {#572e8eae .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.plot(label_by="label", seed=1)
```

```{=html}
<script>
(function(){
  var tip=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('#ec-tooltip-1');
  var svg=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('svg');
  if(!svg||!tip) return;
  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);
      h+='<div><b>'+k+'</b>: '+v+'</div>';
    }
    if(!h) return;
    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mouseout',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge'))
      tip.style.display='none';
  });
})();
</script>
```

The layout treats the edges as springs that pull linked nodes together and the nodes as charges
that push each other apart, so closely knit groups end up near each other. The two halves of the
club are already visible: the instructor, `"0"`, sits among one group on the right, and the
administrator, `"33"`, among the other on the left. Before the drawing is rendered, nodes that would
overlap are pushed apart, and straight edges that would pass through a node are bent around it.

The image is not entirely static: in a notebook or a web page, hovering over a node or an edge shows
a tooltip with its attributes, which makes it easy to identify a node of interest without labelling
every one.

## Displaying and saving plots

`plot()` returns a `StepPlayer` object, the same kind of object that the traversal and step
replays return (see [Traversals](traversals.qmd) and [The step log](step-log.qmd)). Notebooks
and Quarto documents display it automatically when it is the last expression of a cell. Elsewhere,
its `svg` property holds the raw SVG markup as a string:

::: {#f56d4312 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
player = karate.plot(seed=1)
player, player.svg[:60]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3}
```
(StepPlayer(28986 chars),
 '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="700" height="')
```
:::
:::


There are two ways to save a drawing to a file. The `output=` argument saves it as part of the call,
and the `save()` method saves an existing plot. In both cases, a path ending in `.html` writes a
small web page that keeps the hover tooltips, and any other extension writes the plain SVG, which
can be opened by vector graphics editors and placed in documents and slides:

::: {#0e77cc6b .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
karate.plot(label_by="label", seed=1, output="karate.svg")

player = karate.plot(label_by="label", seed=1)
player.save("karate.html")
```
:::


The plot is returned either way, so `output=` can be used in a notebook cell that also displays the
plot.

## Canvas and node size

The canvas is 700 by 500 pixels by default, and `width=` and `height=` change it. The force and
random layouts spread the nodes over the whole canvas, so a wide canvas gives a wide drawing, and
the force layout is turned so that a long graph lies along the canvas's longer side. Positions from
a layout method keep their proportions (see [Layouts](layouts.qmd)).

The node radius is chosen automatically from the canvas area and the number of nodes, from 16 pixels
on small graphs down to 3.5 pixels on large ones, and edge widths likewise shrink as the graph grows.
The defaults, `node_size=16` and `edge_width=1.2`, stand for "automatic"; any other value is used as
given. Smaller nodes leave more room for the edges, which helps on graphs where the structure of the
links matters more than the individual nodes. The 62 bottlenose dolphins of Doubtful Sound, drawn
with small nodes and no labels:

::: {#6c1b10cc .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
dolphins = ec.dolphins()
dolphins.plot(show_labels=False, node_size=7, seed=1)
```

```{=html}
(function(){
  var tip=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('#ec-tooltip-3');
  var svg=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('svg');
  if(!svg||!tip) return;
  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);
      h+='<div><b>'+k+'</b>: '+v+'</div>';

    if(!h) return;
    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mouseout',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;

  });
})();
```

The drawing shows the two communities of the dolphin population, linked by only a few animals.
`edge_opacity=`, 0.4 by default, controls how transparent the edges are. Translucent edges keep
dense regions readable, since areas where many edges cross appear darker rather than solid.

## Node labels

The text drawn on each node is chosen by `label_by=`:

- `"id"` shows the node IDs, which is the default
- `"label"` shows the node labels, or the ID of nodes without a label
- the name of a node attribute shows its value, or the ID of nodes without the attribute
- `"degree"` shows the number of edges of each node

`show_labels=False` turns the text off altogether, which suits graphs with more than a few dozen
nodes, where labels would cover each other. A name that no node has is an error rather than being
silently ignored, so a misspelled attribute is caught immediately:

::: {#6b1e8cba .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
try:
    karate.plot(label_by="faktion")
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
label_by='faktion': no node has an attribute 'faktion' (built-in options are 'id', 'label' and 'degree')
```
:::
:::


Passing `label_by=` on every call gets repetitive when a graph should always be shown with its
labels. [`set_node_attr_to_display()`](../reference/Graph.set_node_attr_to_display.qmd) records a
preference on the graph itself, which `plot()` then uses whenever `label_by=` isn't given:

::: {#bc29a288 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
florentine = ec.florentine_families()
florentine.set_node_attr_to_display("label")
florentine.plot(seed=1)
```

## Directed graphs and multigraphs

A directed graph is drawn with an arrowhead at the target end of each edge. Graphs with parallel
edges, reciprocal edges, and self-loops need some care, since a straight line can show only one edge
between two nodes; `plot()` fans parallel and reciprocal edges out as separate curves, and draws a
self-loop as a small loop above its node. A small supply network has all three:

::: {#f61403d9 .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
supply = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_edges(
    [
        ("Farm", "Mill"),
        ("Farm", "Mill"),
        ("Mill", "Bakery"),
        ("Mill", "Cafe"),
        ("Bakery", "Cafe"),
        ("Cafe", "Bakery"),
        ("Cafe", "Cafe"),
    ],
    auto_create_nodes=True,
)
supply.plot(label_by="label", seed=1, width=500, height=350)
```

## Edge labels

`edge_label_by=` names an edge attribute to write along each edge, which is useful when the edges
are of several kinds or carry a value worth reading. Edges without the attribute are left
unlabelled. In a small organization, some edges record who manages whom and others who mentors whom:

::: {#f7c3d0c3 .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
org = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_edges(
    [
        ("Dana", "Eli"),
        ("Dana", "Fay"),
        ("Eli", "Gus"),
        ("Eli", "Hal"),
        ("Fay", "Ivy"),
        ("Gus", "Hal"),
        ("Fay", "Eli"),
    ],
    auto_create_nodes=True,
)
org.set_edge_attrs("rel", "manages", edge_ids=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
org.set_edge_attrs("rel", "mentors", edge_ids=[6, 7])
org.plot(label_by="label", edge_label_by="rel", seed=1, width=500, height=350)
```

## Choosing a layout

The `layout=` argument chooses how the nodes are placed:

- `"force"`, the default, is a force-directed layout that places linked nodes near each other
- `"circular"` places the nodes evenly around a circle
- `"random"` scatters the nodes uniformly over the canvas
- any other string names a node attribute that holds `(x, y)` coordinates

The circular layout ignores the structure of the graph entirely, which is sometimes the point: it
shows every edge as a chord of the circle, so dense and sparse patterns are easy to compare, and the
positions don't depend on a random seed:

::: {#c9764c3b .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
florentine.plot(layout="circular")
```

The order of the nodes around the circle follows the graph's internal storage order. A
deliberate order, in which linked nodes sit close together, concentrates the edges along the rim
and makes the drawing much easier to read; [Layouts](layouts.qmd#circles-and-shells) shows how
to arrange the circle in a chosen order. The fourth option is the most flexible. The `layout_*()` methods, such as
[`layout_kamada_kawai()`](../reference/Graph.layout_kamada_kawai.qmd) or
[`layout_bipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_bipartite.qmd), compute positions with more
specialized algorithms and store them in the `"pos"` node attribute, which `layout="pos"` then
draws. Positions that come with the data, such as geographic coordinates, can be stored and drawn
the same way. [Layouts](layouts.qmd) describes all of them.

### Reproducible drawings

The force and random layouts start from random positions, so two calls give different pictures
unless `seed=` is passed. The same seed on the same graph always gives the same picture, which is
what a document or a report needs: the text can then refer to the left or the right of the drawing.
Different seeds give drawings that are rotated, reflected, or arranged differently, and it is
worth trying a few seeds when a drawing will be published, since some arrangements show the
structure more clearly than others.

## Curved edges

`curved_edges=True` draws every edge as a gentle curve rather than a straight line. Curves make it
easier to follow individual edges where many of them meet at a node, and give a softer look:

::: {#5c5dc245 .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
florentine.plot(curved_edges=True, seed=1)
```

```{=html}
(function(){

  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];

    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
```

With curved edges, the edges are no longer routed around the nodes, and parallel edges between the
same two nodes are drawn along the same curve, so straight edges are the better choice for
multigraphs.

## Overlaps and edge routing

Two adjustments are made after the layout and before drawing, and both can be turned off or tuned.

`node_overlap=` controls overlapping nodes. The default, `"remove"`, pushes nodes apart until they
are at least 2 pixels from each other, and a number sets a different minimum gap. `"allow"` keeps
the positions exactly as the layout computed them. The adjustment applies to the force and random
layouts, and not to positions given by a `"pos"` attribute, which are taken to be meaningful.

`edge_routing=` controls edges that pass through nodes. The default, `"around"`, bends such an edge
so that it clears the nodes in its way by 3 pixels, and a number sets the clearance. `"straight"`
draws every edge as a direct line. Turning both adjustments off shows the raw layout of the dolphin
network:

::: {#ae3c7143 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
dolphins.plot(show_labels=False, node_size=7, node_overlap="allow", edge_routing="straight", seed=1)
```

```{=html}
<script>
(function(){
  var tip=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('#ec-tooltip-9');
  var svg=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('svg');
  if(!svg||!tip) return;
  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);
      h+='<div><b>'+k+'</b>: '+v+'</div>';
    }
    if(!h) return;
    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mouseout',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge'))
      tip.style.display='none';
  });
})();
</script>
```

The positions are the same as in the earlier dolphin plot, but the nodes in the dense center now
overlap, and some edges run underneath nodes that they don't belong to. The raw layout is faster to
compute, and it is the faithful choice when the distances between nodes are meant to be read,
since overlap removal moves nodes slightly.

dark-mode notebooks and presentation slides. The co-appearance network of the characters of *Les

```{=html}
(function(){
  var tip=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('#ec-tooltip-10');
  var svg=document.currentScript.parentElement.querySelector('svg');

  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');
    if(!raw) return;
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);
      h+='<div><b>'+k+'</b>: '+v+'</div>';

    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';

  svg.addEventListener('mouseout',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;

  });
})();
```

The bishop Myriel and the minor characters of his story form the fan on the left, linked to the
rest of the novel only through Myriel himself. Valjean is the hub at the center, and the dense
cluster to the lower right holds Marius and the students of the ABC society. The theme changes only the background, the default node and edge colors, and
the text; the palettes for colored nodes are described in [Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd).

## Larger graphs

`plot()` works well up to a few hundred nodes and a few thousand edges. Beyond that, two things go
wrong. The drawing becomes a dense ball in which little can be seen, and the force-directed layout,
which considers every pair of nodes, becomes slow: the 4,941 nodes of the power grid network take
about twenty seconds. For the 198 musicians and 2,743 collaborations of the jazz network, small
nodes, no labels, and faint edges are already needed:

::: {#37d3e277 .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
jazz = ec.jazz()
jazz.plot(show_labels=False, node_size=4, edge_opacity=0.15, edge_routing="straight", seed=1)
```

```{=html}
  function show(el,ev){
    var raw=el.getAttribute('data-attrs');

    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);
```

A dense core of musicians who played with many others is surrounded by a sparser periphery. Edge
routing is turned off here: in a dense graph almost every edge passes some node, and the detours
make the drawing busier and the SVG several times larger without making it clearer. For graphs of
this size and larger, several strategies help:

- draw a meaningful part of the graph, such as a k-core, an ego network, or one community, with
  the methods of [Transforming graphs](transforming.qmd)
- collapse groups of nodes into single nodes with `quotient_graph()`, so that the drawing shows how
  the groups are linked
- color the nodes by community or size them by centrality, so that the structure stands out even
  when individual nodes can't be told apart (see [Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd))
- use `plot_cosmo()`, which lays out and draws graphs of hundreds of thousands of nodes on the GPU
  in the browser (see [Interactive widgets](interactive.qmd))

## Summary

| Argument | Controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `layout=` | node placement: `"force"`, `"circular"`, `"random"`, or a position attribute | `"force"` |
| `seed=` | the random start of the force and random layouts | `None` |
| `width=`, `height=` | canvas size in pixels | `600`, `400` |
| `node_size=`, `edge_width=` | node radius and edge width, automatic at their defaults | `16`, `1.2` |
| `edge_opacity=` | edge transparency, from 0 to 1 | `0.4` |
| `label_by=`, `show_labels=` | the node text | `None`, `True` |
| `edge_label_by=` | an edge attribute to write along the edges | `None` |
| `curved_edges=` | curved rather than straight edges | `False` |
| `node_overlap=`, `edge_routing=` | overlap removal and routing around nodes | `"remove"`, `"around"` |
| `theme=` | `"light"` or `"dark"` | `"light"` |
| `output=` | a path to save to, as `.svg` or `.html` | `None` |

The arguments for colors and sizes, `color_by=`, `size_by=`, `edge_color_by=`, `palette=`, and
`cross_community_color=`, are covered in [Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd).
